headline_en: Demand exists in South Korea, but workers cannot be sent
summary_en: South Korean farms regularly ask for seasonal (part-time) workers with employer-paid travel, lodging and high pay, but private Bangladeshi recruiting agencies cannot send anyone because Korea issues the E-8 seasonal visa only where a memorandum exists with a Korean local government. One agency, KM International, got demand letters for 80 workers attested and ministry approval but the Korean embassy issued no visas. The expatriates' welfare ministry says it is working on an MoU and will hold an inter-ministerial meeting.

facts.statement: As of April 2024 private Bangladeshi recruiting agencies could not send seasonal (part-time) workers to South Korea because of approval and visa complications, although demand for such workers comes in regularly.

Besides government-to-government hiring, South Korea takes agricultural workers through its local government bodies; for this the Korean local government institution must sign a memorandum of understanding with the sending country's local government division. As of April 2024 Bangladesh was in talks to sign such an MoU.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment sources

facts.statement: South Korea takes seasonal workers for jobs such as dried-fish processing, vegetable gardening and marketing, and pig farming; workers from Sri Lanka, Nepal, Vietnam, China, the Philippines, India and some other countries currently go for these jobs.

Private recruiting agency KM International received demand for more than 2,000 workers for South Korea in 2023 and collected passports from 700 interested workers. In two phases the labour wing of the Bangladesh embassy in Korea verified and attested demand letters for 80 workers and wrote to the ministry, which approved sending them, but the Korean embassy issued no visa to any worker.

The Korean embassy refused visas to KM International's workers because their appointment letters were for 90 days, which needs a C-4-5 visa (three months only) that Korea is not giving to anyone for worker recruitment. Korea approves the E-8 visa for seasonal workers, which allows eight months of work, but that visa requires an agreement with Korea's local government division.

First Secretary (Labour) Mikon Tongchongya of the Bangladesh embassy in Korea said the embassy physically inspected the employer's establishment and verified all papers before attesting the demand letters, but did not attest the visa matter; sending workers needs an E-8 visa, for which the expatriates' welfare ministry must sign an MoU with Korea's local government division, and the ministry is working on it.
facts.source_in_article: Mikon Tongchongya, First Secretary (Labour), Bangladesh embassy in South Korea

facts.statement: KM International said repeated talks with various levels of the Korean and Bangladeshi governments did not solve the problem, so it returned the passports collected from interested workers. It said Korean employers are still in contact, there is scope to send more than 15,000 workers, and it is waiting for the agreement to be signed.

Hampyeong-gun (হামপিয়াং-গুন) local government of South Korea signed an MoU with Chapainawabganj Zila Parishad to take workers; recruiting agency Hope Human Resources has been trying to send seasonal workers to it and wrote to the expatriates' welfare ministry several times, but could not send workers because of Korea's rules.

According to BMET, 4,996 workers went to South Korea in various sectors in 2023, of whom 4,804 were sent by the state agency Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL); only a few went through private recruiting agencies.

Private-sector recruiters say seasonal farm work in South Korea lets a worker stay eight months at a time, take three months' leave and return for another eight months; the employer pays the airfare for the leave trips, monthly pay is more than 1.5 lakh taka, and there is no requirement to learn Korean or have technical knowledge. The article's lead also says travel, lodging and food are at the employer's cost.
The Korean embassy is not issuing visas for any job of less than one year, which is why sending seasonal workers is stuck.

Additional Secretary (Employment) Khairul Alam of the expatriates' welfare ministry said the ministry is working on sending seasonal workers to Korea and an inter-ministerial meeting would be held soon to decide next steps.

OKUP chairperson Shakirul Islam said the farm-work opportunity in Korea can be taken up but must be carefully vetted, the benefits promised to workers must be ensured, no risk should be created for the Korean labour market, and no worker should be cheated.
facts.source_in_article: Shakirul Islam, chairperson, Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program (OKUP)

headline_en: Why don't we emphasise language teaching to raise remittances from the Middle East
summary_en: A reader's letter by a university student argues that Bangladeshi workers in the Middle East earn and remit less because they lack language skills, and proposes Arabic-language and technical courses, including through madrasas and school curricula. It cites BMET, IOM and Gulf expatriate-share figures.

facts.statement: According to BMET, from 1976 until about March 2024 a total of 1 crore 45 lakh 8 thousand (14,508,000) Bangladeshis went abroad with BMET clearance, of whom 51 lakh 82 thousand (5,182,000) went to Saudi Arabia.

The letter writer says most Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia start in gardening, as street cleaners or as domestic workers, work that is hard in the desert heat and low paid, and that women workers face more hardship.

OKUP chairman Shakirul Islam, quoted from a 2023 Business Standard Bangla report, said women domestic workers in the Middle East face physical abuse and other problems mainly because they do not know the language, while most men work in manufacturing, construction and services and, though not directly troubled by language, lag in remittance; with the local language they could get better jobs and earn more, as seen with workers from Sri Lanka, the Philippines and India.
facts.source_in_article: Shakirul Islam, OKUP, via Business Standard Bangla (2023)

facts.statement: According to 2019 IOM data cited in the letter, a Bangladeshi migrant worker sends home on average USD 203.33 a month, against USD 546.10 for a Filipino worker.

The letter cites a Daily Star column saying Filipino migrants, because of English skills, work in hotels and restaurants, as shopping-mall sales staff or as babysitters, jobs that are less strenuous and better paid, so their remittances are higher although Bangladeshi workers are more numerous.
facts.source_in_article: Daily Star column, cited by letter writer

facts.statement: BMET data cited in the letter: 24 lakh 85 thousand (2,485,000) Bangladeshis have gone to the United Arab Emirates since 1976, 17.13 percent of all those going abroad with BMET clearance; the UAE is Bangladesh's second-largest labour market, and more than 10 lakh Bangladeshis still live there.

Expatriate share of population in the six Gulf Cooperation Council countries as given in the letter: UAE 88.5 percent, Qatar 85.7 percent, Kuwait about 69.2 percent, Bahrain 52 percent, Oman 44 percent, Saudi Arabia 32.7 percent.

The letter writer recommends government and private courses, including Arabic-language courses, for people going to the Middle East, wide publicity for them, a technical course in madrasas, and an Arabic speaking/writing component in school Islam and moral education (for example 30 of 100 marks practical).
facts.source_in_article: letter writer Sheikh Saimon Parvez, pharmacy student, Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University

headline_en: Eight Bangladeshis killed in boat accident off Tunisia identified
summary_en: Eight of the nine people killed when a migrant boat caught fire off Tunisia on 15 February 2024 were Bangladeshis heading from Libya to Europe. The Bangladesh embassy in Libya named the eight, from Madaripur and Gopalganj, and said the Tunisian navy rescued 26 Bangladeshis.

facts.statement: On 15 February 2024 a boat carrying about 52 migrants of various nationalities from the Libyan coast towards Europe caught fire at sea off the Tunisian coast; at least 9 people died, 8 of them Bangladeshis and one a Pakistani national.

The Bangladesh embassy in Libya identified the eight Bangladeshi dead as: Nayan Biswas of Kadambari, Mamun Sheikh and Sajal of Khalia, Kazi Sajib of Bajitpur Notunbazar and Kaisar of Kabirajpur, all in Rajoir upazila, Madaripur; and Rifat of Ragdi, Rasel of Dignagar and Imrul Kayes alias Apon of Gangarampur Gohala, in Muksudpur upazila, Gopalganj.
The Tunisian navy rescued 26 Bangladeshis from the burning boat; one was in critical condition.
The victims were travelling by sea from the Libyan coast across the Mediterranean towards Europe.
The Bangladesh embassy in Libya said it was in contact with Tunisian authorities, the International Red Crescent Society and IOM for the rescue and medical treatment of the Bangladeshis.

headline_en: Saudi Arabia to take doctors and nurses from Bangladesh
summary_en: Citing Arab News, the article reports that Saudi Arabia has begun recruiting Bangladeshi medical workers after a 2022 agreement, with a first group of about 60 going in November 2023 and a nurses' group next. Saudi authorities asked for more than 150 trained nurses and the Bangladeshi ministry is vetting the demand and preparing procedures.

facts.statement: Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia signed an agreement in 2022 on recruiting Bangladeshi medical workers; the first group, of about 60 Bangladeshi medical workers, went to Saudi Arabia in November 2023.
facts.source_in_article: Arab News report cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Saudi ambassador in Dhaka Essa Al-Duhailan told Arab News (interview published about 2 February 2024) that Saudi Arabia had not recruited medical workers from Bangladesh for a long time but has now started because they meet Saudi standards; the first group is only a beginning and the number will jump in the near future.
facts.source_in_article: Essa Al-Duhailan, Saudi ambassador in Dhaka, to Arab News

facts.statement: A team from the Saudi health ministry visited Bangladesh twice in 2023 and will keep visiting to recruit more medical workers.

The next group to go from Bangladesh to Saudi Arabia will be nurses; Saudi authorities asked Bangladesh to send more than 150 trained nurses, and the expatriates' welfare ministry is vetting the demand (where they will be posted, whether in government or private hospitals).
facts.source_in_article: Khairul Alam, Additional Secretary, expatriates' welfare ministry, to Arab News

facts.statement: Because recruiting medical workers for Saudi Arabia is new, the Bangladesh government is preparing a working procedure and plans a detailed recruitment policy.
According to the Bangladesh Medical Association, about 30 lakh Bangladeshi workers are in Saudi Arabia, only a few of them medical workers.

headline_en: Lottery for zero-cost recruitment to Malaysia; where the final list will be available
summary_en: BOESL held an electronic lottery on 8 November 2026 to shortlist 300 of 4,029 online applicants for jobs at DHL Supply Chain in Malaysia; 112 who pass practical and oral tests will go with no migration cost. BOESL also has demand letters for 558 more employer-paid jobs in Malaysia.

facts.statement: 112 Bangladeshis are to get jobs at DHL Supply Chain in Malaysia at no migration cost through the state agency BOESL; 300 candidates were first shortlisted by lottery.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Online applications for the DHL Supply Chain Malaysia jobs were received from 6 November until 4pm on 8 November 2026; 4,029 candidates applied. An electronic lottery held at 4:30pm on Sunday 8 November 2026 at the Probashi auditorium of Probashi Kallyan Bhaban shortlisted 300: 200 for Operations Assistant and 100 for Technical Skill Workers.
Shortlisted candidates will sit practical and oral tests held in the presence of DHL Supply Chain representatives; the 112 who finally pass will be sent to Malaysia without any migration cost.
The list of finally selected candidates for the DHL Supply Chain Malaysia jobs will be published on BOESL's website and Facebook page.

BOESL managing director Mohammad Rashedul Haque said this is the first time a lottery has been used to select workers for government-channel recruitment to Malaysia, and flights of the selected workers will start from the first week of December (2026).
facts.source_in_article: Mohammad Rashedul Haque, managing director, BOESL

facts.statement: BOESL has received demand letters for 558 more workers for Malaysia in tourism, manufacturing and caregiving; the employers will bear all costs including medical tests and airfare, so these workers will also go with no migration cost.
facts.source_in_article: Mohammad Rashedul Haque, managing director, BOESL

facts.statement: Acting secretary Ahmadul Haque of the expatriates' welfare ministry said sending one crore workers abroad in the next five years is the current government's election pledge.

headline_en: Some go on a promise of work, some fall for the 'bait' of going to Malaysia free of cost
summary_en: On Thursday 5 November 2026 a joint army, BGB and police operation freed 57 people from a traffickers' den in the deep hills of Rangikhali, Teknaf, where they were held for ransom and due to be put on a trawler to Malaysia that night; a soldier was shot dead. Victims describe being lured by offers of work in Rohingya camps or of going to Malaysia free and paying after arrival, then being sold, beaten and chained.

facts.statement: Nur Kamal (21) of Daganbhuiyan, Feni, said a person added him to a WhatsApp group offering to take him to Malaysia free of cost, with payment only after reaching Malaysia; he left home on 2 November 2026, reached Cox's Bazar on 3 November, and was taken from there and locked in a hut in the Teknaf hills, where beating and torture began.
facts.source_in_article: victim Nur Kamal, speaking at Teknaf police station on 6 November 2026

facts.statement: Tarekul Islam (23), a mason from Gandamara, Banshkhali, Chattogram, said two Rohingya youths he had got to know took him on 2 November 2026 on the promise of bridge-construction work in a Teknaf Rohingya camp, then via Baradeil in Baharchhara union to a den in the deep hills where he was held with 55 to 60 others in one room.

People lured from various areas with job offers or free passage to Malaysia were held in a den in the deep hills of Rangikhali, Teknaf, tortured for ransom, and were to be loaded on a trawler on the night of Thursday 5 November 2026 for trafficking to Malaysia by sea.

On the afternoon of Thursday 5 November 2026 a joint operation by the army's 10 Infantry Division, BGB and police raided the traffickers' den in Teknaf and rescued 57 people; police identified one of them as a trafficker and 56 as victims. 37 were handed to families on the night of 6 November after identity checks and the rest were kept at Teknaf police station; no case had been filed as of 6 November.
facts.source_in_article: Sukanta Chowdhury, Inspector (Investigation), Teknaf police station

facts.statement: During the Teknaf raid there was an exchange of fire with traffickers in which army soldier Md Titas Sheikh (27) was shot dead; five members of the trafficking ring were detained and one pistol, one locally made gun and four rounds were recovered.

S M Asaduzzaman (50) of Saltha, Faridpur, said he met a man named Yamamul at Kutupalong Rohingya camp while visiting, was called on the promise of camp work, taken away on 29 October 2026, robbed of his phone and belongings, and driven at night by CNG auto-rickshaw to the hills where he was handed to traffickers for 10,000 taka.

Asaduzzaman said he made a verbal deal with the traffickers to be freed for 2 lakh taka and they agreed, but the joint forces rescued him first. Two days before the rescue a trawler was preparing to sail and they tried to put him on it with five others, but there was no room.

Asaduzzaman said more than fifty people were held in the hill den under armed guard, and claimed the captors had about 130 machetes (da) and heavy weapons like AK-47s. Nur Kamal said 10 to 12 armed men were always on guard and anyone who said anything against them was beaten.
facts.source_in_article: victims S M Asaduzzaman and Nur Kamal

facts.statement: Md Saiful Islam of Ukhiya said a broker named Nur Ali handed him to traffickers on the promise of work, and the traffickers told him they had bought him and one other person for 1 lakh taka.

Saiful Islam said that over five days he saw four or five new people brought to the den every day; those who tried to talk or escape were badly beaten and then bound with iron chains; food was given twice a day, bottle gourd and dal.

Mohammad Ali, acting chairman of Hnila Union Parishad, Teknaf, said armed groups' activity in the hills is rising and traffickers' movement has increased in the winter season, and called for a sweeping operation.
facts.source_in_article: Mohammad Ali, acting chairman, Hnila UP

headline_en: Two Bangladeshis executed in Saudi Arabia: what a confidential document reveals
summary_en: A confidential 18 October 2026 letter from the labour welfare wing of the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah says the two Bangladeshis executed in the Makkah region, Nazrul Islam Abdul Bashir and Sweety Akter, had been in Saudi jails since August 2023 and that Saudi authorities never informed the mission before or after. The letter also says 306 Bangladeshis are held in western-region jails in morality cases.

facts.statement: Two Bangladeshis, Nazrul Islam Abdul Bashir and Sweety Akter, were executed in the Makkah region of Saudi Arabia; the execution became known from Saudi media reports on 14 October 2026 citing a Saudi interior ministry statement. The charge was violating the sanctity of a mosque in Makkah by engaging in immoral acts inside it.
facts.source_in_article: confidential letter of the Jeddah consulate's labour welfare wing, citing Saudi interior ministry statement

facts.statement: Saudi authorities told the Bangladesh embassy or consulate nothing in advance about the two executions, did not formally inform them afterwards, did not notify them of the verdict, and did not supply detailed information on the two.

According to a prisoner list the Jeddah consulate received from the Saudi foreign ministry on 30 September 2026, Nazrul was detained on 1 August 2023 on an information-technology offence charge and held in Jeddah correctional facility, and Sweety was detained the next day on an adultery charge and held in Jeddah women's prison; the list gave no sentence for either. Both worked as cleaners for a Saudi company named Al Majal.
The Jeddah consulate's letter says there is no precedent of a Bangladeshi being sentenced to death in Saudi Arabia on information-technology or adultery charges.

The list shows 306 Bangladeshis held in jails of Saudi Arabia's western region in various morality-related cases; 147 of them have been sentenced, with terms from a minimum of one month to a maximum of 15 years in prison.

The consulate said it had received no application for legal aid and no contact from the families of the two executed Bangladeshis. It sent a diplomatic note to the Makkah branch of the Saudi foreign ministry for the verdict copy and case details.

headline_en: Recommendation to stop harassment of migrant workers at airports
summary_en: The parliamentary standing committee on the expatriates' welfare ministry on 8 October 2026 recommended watching that migrant workers face no neglect or harassment at airports. The ministry reported 432,786 workers sent abroad from 18 February to 30 September 2026 and 186 people brought back from Iran. facts.statement: The parliamentary standing committee on the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, meeting at Parliament on Thursday 8 October 2026, recommended keeping watch so that migrant workers face no neglect or harassment at airports, and told ministry officials to work carefully so that no irregularity or corruption occurs.

headline_en: Migrant worker deaths: more than 14 bodies a day on average arrived; which country has the most
summary_en: From January to 30 September 2026, 4,060 bodies of migrant workers arrived in Bangladesh, more than 14 a day, most from Saudi Arabia (about 2,000) followed by Malaysia. The article explains how the Wage Earners' Welfare Board repatriates bodies and pays burial, grant and insurance money, the delays for irregular workers and countries with no embassy, and the fact that causes of death reported from abroad are never verified by Bangladesh.

facts.statement: Al Amin of Pabna, who worked at a tiles factory in Cambodia, was crushed under more than a hundred tiles while working and died on 12 April 2025; his body reached Bangladesh on 27 September 2026, about a year and a half later.

Al Amin's brother-in-law Masum Khan applied to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board in Dhaka with help from the NGO BRAC. He said Cambodia has no Bangladesh embassy, so the board sent the application to Thailand; the embassy could not locate the body, and he obtained the local police's number through expatriates there and passed it to the board.
facts.source_in_article: Masum Khan, brother-in-law of the deceased

facts.statement: BRAC Migration Programme says bodies of regular workers come home more or less on time, but when a worker has become irregular (no valid papers) bringing the body takes a long time; some workers in Saudi Arabia are buried locally, but most families want the body brought home.

The Wage Earners' Welfare Board under the expatriates' welfare ministry takes responsibility for bringing home the body of a worker who dies abroad. Board officials say in Middle Eastern countries approval is needed from several offices before a body can be sent, which takes some time though less than before, and that it takes longer from countries with no embassy.

Wage Earners' Welfare Board data: 3,651 migrants' bodies arrived in 2019 and 3,140 in 2020, when many were buried locally during the Covid pandemic; arrivals rose from 2021. Outside the Covid period, fewer than 1 percent of the dead are buried in destination countries.
In the nine months (273 days) from January to 30 September 2026, 4,060 bodies of migrant workers arrived in Bangladesh, an average of more than 14 a day.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board data via reporter

facts.statement: The most workers died in Saudi Arabia, about 2,000 in 2026 so far; Saudi Arabia is also the largest destination and received the most workers in 2026. Malaysia had the second-highest number of deaths, although recruitment to Malaysia has been closed for the past two and a half years.

NGO and research officials say the destination country sends a written cause of death, in most cases shown as natural death including illness; there are allegations of workplace abuse, murder and forced suicide, but Bangladesh does not verify any cause of death of workers abroad.
facts.source_in_article: officials of NGOs and research bodies working on migration

facts.statement: Expatriates' welfare minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said on 1 October 2026 that since the BNP government took office medical assistance for migrants has been increased, steps have been taken to bring bodies home quickly including those of irregular workers, and what to do to verify causes of death abroad will be decided.

The worker's family must apply to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board after a death. If the worker went abroad with BMET clearance, or took membership registration from the embassy after going abroad, the board pays the cost of bringing the body home. If neither applies the family can still apply; the board then sends a proposal to the expatriates' welfare ministry, which pays the repatriation cost from a yearly budget allocation.

Ministry data: previously about 70 percent of papers arriving with bodies gave natural death as the cause; in the first nine months of 2026, 66 percent were recorded as natural and the other 34 percent died from accidents and other causes. More than 16 percent died in 2026 from road accidents, workplace accidents, burns, falls from buildings and electrocution.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment

facts.statement: A 2023 Wage Earners' Welfare Board analysis: 18,166 bodies arrived in the five years 2018 to 2022; 3,698 died from road accidents, workplace accidents, burns, falls from buildings and electric shock, of whom 2,649 died in road accidents; more than 20 percent in all died in accidents linked to work, occurring on the way to and from work and at work.

Brothers Foyez Ahmed (10 years in Saudi Arabia) and Sujon Ahmed (joined him seven months earlier) of Noakhali, who transported dates in the same vehicle, died in a road accident in Saudi Arabia on 16 July 2026; their bodies arrived on 28 July. Their father Abdul Malek said the board gave 35,000 taka each, 70,000 taka in all, for burial.

For every body that arrives in Bangladesh the Wage Earners' Welfare Board gives 35,000 taka in cash for burial, followed by a financial grant of 3 lakh taka. In addition the worker's family now gets life-insurance benefit, and any compensation claim abroad and the dead worker's unpaid dues are recovered through the embassy.

Welfare board data for the first six months of 2026: 9 crore 45 lakh taka paid for burial of bodies, 61 crore 56 lakh taka in financial grants, more than 44 crore taka in insurance benefits to workers, and about 75 crore taka in compensation, dues and insurance recovered from abroad.

People in the sector say that after applying, families have to visit the Welfare Board day after day and some families are in dire straits by the time help arrives; irregular workers who return from abroad having lost everything do not get these government benefits.

Migration research bodies say a large share of Bangladeshi workers in the Middle East work in infrastructure construction in extreme daytime heat; heat-related illness damages kidneys, the brain and other organs, creates long-term health risks needing lifelong treatment, can worsen respiratory, heart, diabetes and kidney disease and causes premature death, and climate change is raising the heat.

Ministry officials say BMET's pre-departure training is only a three-day workshop covering destination rules, conduct and safety awareness, in which nothing is taught well; training is needed on the type of work, environment, coping with pressure, working hours and how to stay healthy.

BRAC Migration Programme head Shariful Hasan said deaths rise every year, young men of 25 to 30 are dying, and more than 70 percent of bodies come from the Middle East, most from Saudi Arabia; he said every death's cause should be investigated, women's suicides especially, and the state must take responsibility for bringing home even an irregular worker's body without delay.
facts.source_in_article: Shariful Hasan, head, BRAC Migration Programme

headline_en: After Mediterranean boat sinking, two young men from the same Bhairab village rescued, one missing
summary_en: Three young men from Adarshapara village, Bhairab, Kishoreganj, were on a boat that left Libya for Greece on 14 September 2026 and sank south of Gavdos island; two are alive in Greek custody and one, Bayezid Mia, is missing. Families say a local broker contracted to deliver each to Greece for 14 lakh taka, routing them via Saudi Arabia (Umrah), Egypt and Libya.

facts.statement: A boat that left Libya on the night of 14 September 2026 for Greece sank south of Greece's Gavdos island; according to AFP it carried 77 people, 51 were rescued, one body was found and 25 are missing.

Families in Bhairab, Kishoreganj, say local broker Sohag Mia contracted to deliver each of three young men to Greece for 14 lakh taka: 9 lakh taka was taken first and the remaining 5 lakh taka was due after reaching Greece. Bayezid's family raised the 9 lakh taka from savings and loans.

Bayezid and Kawsar left Bangladesh about a month and a half before 23 September 2026 and Rahim a month before them. They were first taken to Saudi Arabia, where they performed Umrah, then via Egypt to Libya, where they stayed more than a month before the boat left for Greece on the night of 14 September.

Sohag Mia, a local broker whose home is in Shambhupur Alukanda area of Shibpur union, Bhairab upazila, Kishoreganj, is named by the families as the person through whom the contract to reach Greece was made.

Survivors Rahim Mia (24) and Kawsar Mia (25) of Adarshapara, Kalikaprasad union, Bhairab, are in the custody of Greek law-enforcement; both phoned home after midnight on Sunday 20 September 2026. Rahim said a ship rescued them and he stayed on the ship several days.

Bayezid Mia (20) of Adarshapara, Bhairab, has been untraced since the sinking; neither his family nor the upazila administration has confirmation of his death. The three swam together for a while after the boat sank and then lost each other.
facts.source_in_article: family; Bhairab UNO K M Mamunur Rashid

facts.statement: Kawsar Mia, a farmer, used family savings and also borrowed 4 lakh taka to go abroad.

Bayezid went to Qatar while in class ten, could not make it work there and returned after six months, then planned to go to Europe; his elder brother Raihan lives in Italy. Rahim has two brothers in Italy.

summary_en: The Bangladesh embassy in Cairo said on 16 August 2026 that 29 Bangladeshis were rescued alive from a rubber boat that left Tobruk, Libya, for Greece on 3 August, ran out of fuel and drifted about 10 days to Marsa Matruh, Egypt. facts.statement: Greek newspaper Dimokratia reported that at least 202 migrants reached the island of Crete in successive boat journeys from Libya in less than 48 hours; most were nationals of Bangladesh and Sudan, with some Egyptians.

facts.statement: On the morning of Thursday 6 August 2026 a boat with 40 migrants reached Ierapetra in south-east Crete after a Frontex aircraft spotted it; a coast guard patrol vessel and a fishing boat took them to Ierapetra port, where they were registered and identity checks began.
A few hours earlier 112 migrants arrived in two boats: the first carried 56 people (31 Sudanese, 25 Bangladeshis) and the second 56 people (47 Bangladeshis, 9 Egyptians).
All the rescued migrants were placed in a temporary shelter camp at Heraklion port in Crete, where new arrivals are being kept as migrant numbers on the island grow.

facts.statement: The article says illegal human trafficking by sea through the Teknaf-Ukhiya coast of Cox's Bazar keeps increasing, with incidents almost every day and growing casualties from trawler sinkings in the deep sea.

BRAC Migration Programme, with Australian government support, held a 100-km safe-migration road show under the slogan 'No going abroad by sea' (সমুদ্রপথে বিদেশ না) from Ukhiya (10am) via Teknaf and Marine Drive to Kolatoli, Cox's Bazar (8pm), part of a four-day 'Mass Campaign to Combat Human Trafficking and People Smuggling' also held in Gazipur, Dhaka and Narayanganj. Ukhiya police sub-inspector Palash Barua warned that many people from the Cox's Bazar area become trafficking victims when trying to go abroad by sea out of greed; every year many die or go missing in accidents on this route and their families are left destitute.

headline_en: Six young men from Cumilla held hostage in a 'mafia' den in Libya; torture shown on video calls
summary_en: Six young men from Manoharganj upazila, Cumilla, who paid a local broker 18 to 20 lakh taka each to reach Italy via Libya, have been in Libya about eight months and for 15 to 20 days have been hostages of a 'mafia' ring that tortures them on video and demands 27 lakh taka each. Families complained to the foreign ministry; the accused broker's family has gone into hiding and no written complaint has been filed at the police station.

facts.statement: Six young men from Manoharganj upazila, Cumilla, who left illegally through a local broker to reach Italy, have been in Libya about eight to nine months and about 15 to 20 days before 23 July 2026 were taken hostage by a 'mafia' trafficking ring that tortures them daily.

facts.statement: The ring in Libya demands a ransom of 27 lakh taka per person for the six Cumilla men, saying it will send them back to Bangladesh if paid and threatening to kill them and float the bodies in the sea if not.

facts.statement: Each of the six was charged 18 to 20 lakh taka by the broker under a deal to send them from Libya to Italy by sea. Mahbubur Rahman said broker Manik took 20 lakh taka from him through his brother Samsul Alam about nine months earlier; Shah Alam said he paid 18 lakh taka eight months earlier through Samsul Alam. Families paid by borrowing and selling land.
facts.source_in_article: Harunur Rashid; fathers Mahbubur Rahman and Shah Alam

facts.statement: Families allege the men were taken to Libya on the promise of Italy, kept in various places for about eight months, then handed by the broker ring to another broker or mafia ring; torture videos and photos are sent to families on imo and WhatsApp, sometimes shown on live video calls, to extract ransom. Families suspect the brokers cooperated in the hostage-taking.

Manik, son of Belal Hossain of Dishaband village, Khila union, Manoharganj, Cumilla, sends people abroad and lives in Libya; his brother Samsul Alam works for him in Bangladesh and collected the money. Manik told villagers he would arrange 'big jobs' in Italy. After the torture videos spread, Samsul Alam and family members left the area and went into hiding, with phones switched off.
About a week before 23 July 2026 the victims' families filed a complaint with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs seeking redress but had heard of no effective action.

Manoharganj police station officer-in-charge Maksud Ahmed said he had heard of the incident through various channels but no one had filed a written complaint at the station; action would follow investigation if a complaint is received.

headline_en: Half of remittances come from six Middle East countries
summary_en: A Bangladesh Bank report shows the six Gulf countries supply nearly half of Bangladesh's remittances (47 percent, USD 4.8 billion, in October-December), and warns that a prolonged Middle East war would cut inflows. The article gives remittance by country, worker departures last year and worker stocks in each Gulf country, and says five Bangladeshis have died in the war so far.

facts.date: fiscal year printed as 2026-27, July-September and October-December quarters
facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank's report shows the six Gulf countries (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain, Kuwait) supplied 45 percent of total remittances in the first quarter (July-September) and 47 percent in the second quarter (October-December) of the current fiscal year, which the article prints as 2026-27 although it was published in March 2026; in 2020-21 the share was 60 percent and it fell steadily after.

In the second quarter USD 867 crore of remittances arrived, of which USD 480 crore (47 percent) came from the six Gulf countries: Saudi Arabia USD 131 crore, UAE USD 118 crore, Oman USD 51 crore, Kuwait USD 44 crore, Qatar USD 42 crore, Bahrain USD 23 crore. (The six country figures as printed add up to less than USD 480 crore.)

After the Gulf six, the European Union supplied 19.61 percent (USD 170 crore) of remittances, Asia-Pacific countries 15.60 percent, the United States 7.59 percent, and other countries the remaining 10 percent.
In 2025 a total of 11 lakh 16 thousand workers went abroad from Bangladesh: 7 lakh 43 thousand to Saudi Arabia, 1 lakh 7 thousand to Qatar, 40 thousand to Kuwait and 13 thousand to the UAE.

Expatriates' welfare ministry figures for Bangladeshi workers currently in the Gulf: Saudi Arabia about 20 lakh, UAE 10 lakh, Oman 7 lakh, Qatar 4 lakh 50 thousand, Bahrain 1 lakh 50 thousand, Kuwait 1 lakh 40 thousand.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment

facts.statement: The United States and Israel jointly attacked Iran on 28 February 2026 and the war spread to other Middle East countries, with Iranian attacks on US bases and installations in various Gulf countries; five Bangladeshis had died in this war as of 20 March 2026.
Despite the war, USD 220 crore of remittances arrived in the first two weeks of March 2026, USD 113 crore of it in the second week.

Bangladesh Bank's report warns that if the Middle East war is prolonged remittances from the region will fall significantly and pressure on the economy will rise; if it ends quickly the effect will be small.

headline_en: Financial assistance will be arranged for migrants killed during the Middle East war: expatriates' welfare minister
summary_en: Receiving at Sylhet airport on 9 March 2026 the body of Ahmad Ali, killed in a bomb attack in Dubai, minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said four Bangladeshis had died in the Middle East war so far and their families would get government financial help. Officials described the crisis teams, hotline 16135 for cancelled flights, a planned request to extend expired visas, and possible charter flights if the situation worsens.

facts.statement: The expatriates' welfare minister confirmed that four Bangladeshi citizens had died because of the war in the Middle East as of 9 March 2026: two in Saudi Arabia, one in Bahrain and one in Dubai, UAE. Besides Ahmad Ali of Barlekha, one was from Kishoreganj, one from Tangail and one from Sandwip, Chattogram.

Ahmad Ali (Saleh Ahmad) of Gazitaka (গাজিটেকা) (Banshtala) village, Barlekha, was killed in a bomb attack in Dubai and was the first Bangladeshi to die in the war; his body was flown first to Dhaka and then received at Sylhet Osmani International Airport on Monday 9 March 2026. He had been abroad 27 years and left a wife, three sons and a daughter.

The minister said the government would arrange financial assistance, as far as it is able, for the families of migrants killed during the Middle East war; of the four dead, one body had been brought home and the others would follow.

The minister said the foreign ministry, expatriates' welfare ministry and civil aviation are working jointly: a crisis team of the three ministries was formed, there is a hotline, sick and injured Bangladeshis are being treated in hospitals there through the consulates, and the ministry holds details such as passport numbers and home locations of those affected.

Because Bangladesh has no consulate in Lebanon (as the minister put it), the International Labour Organization (ILO) has been given responsibility there; daily information is taken through the ILO and services to Bangladeshi citizens are arranged through it.

Senior secretary Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan said that if the war situation worsens, migrants in the Middle East will be brought home if needed, including by chartered aircraft; saving lives comes first and compensation can be dealt with after the situation normalises.
facts.source_in_article: Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan, senior secretary, expatriates' welfare ministry

facts.statement: Information on people whose flights were cancelled because of the Middle East war is being collected through hotline 16135; they will be contacted and informed when flights resume.
For workers whose visas have expired (during the flight disruption), the Bangladesh government will request extension of visa validity; this was in process as of 9 March 2026.
The minister said some migrants still cannot leave their homes because of the war and that drone attacks are happening even in front of the homes of Bangladeshi consulate staff.

headline_en: Probashi Kallyan Bank giving loans up to 10 lakh taka for acquiring skills abroad
summary_en: Probashi Kallyan Bank has launched an easy-term loan of 1 to 10 lakh taka at 11 percent interest for students and trainees going abroad for language and skills courses, especially to Japan, Germany, South Korea, Italy and Russia. The article lists eligibility, documents, collateral tiers and the bank's fraud warning and helpline 16238.

facts.statement: Probashi Kallyan Bank has launched a loan for language learning and special skills to widen overseas employment: students and trainees going abroad can borrow 1 lakh to 10 lakh taka for a term of two to five years at 11 percent interest, a rate that may change. The loan can be taken from any branch of the bank.

The Probashi Kallyan Bank skills loan is for students and trainees wishing to join language and skills training courses abroad with a view to overseas employment, especially in Japan, Germany, South Korea, Italy and Russia, and applies only to short courses of at most two years.

Eligibility for the Probashi Kallyan Bank skills loan: the applicant must be a local resident, be no older than 40, hold an offer letter (admission confirmation) issued by the educational institution in the destination country, and hold at least an intermediate-level language certificate accepted in the destination country, for example N-4 for Japan or TOPIK Level 3 for South Korea.

Documents for the Probashi Kallyan Bank skills loan: three recent passport-size photos, photocopy of national ID, the foreign institution's offer letter, photocopies of passport and latest academic certificate, the language certificate, and the name, address and documents of one guarantor able to repay (a family member or relative may be guarantor).

Collateral for the Probashi Kallyan Bank skills loan: 1 to 3 lakh taka needs no collateral, only one guarantor's personal guarantee and three cheque leaves from the guarantor's active bank account; 3 to 5 lakh taka needs the original deed of immovable property worth at least twice the loan limit deposited at the branch plus the guarantor's guarantee and three cheque leaves; 5 to 10 lakh taka needs a registered mortgage and an irrevocable power of attorney in the bank's favour on immovable property worth at least twice the loan limit.
Probashi Kallyan Bank warns of fraud in the loan process: it has no agents, and loan applications can be made only online or directly at the nearest branch.
Probashi Kallyan Bank helpline for any information or help: 16238.

Bdjobs chief executive Fahim Mashroor said 12 lakh people go abroad each year and 90 to 95 percent of them have only secondary-level education; he said low-skilled labour export should be temporarily banned and that learning a foreign language and gaining minimum skills leads to better jobs.

headline_en: Must we die by missile in Ukraine and by pirates' bullets in the Mediterranean?
summary_en: A column by Prothom Alo editorial assistant Monoj Dey on young Bangladeshis dying on the Libya-Mediterranean route to Italy and as contract fighters for Russia in Ukraine. It recounts November 2025 deaths off Libya, the sums paid to brokers under 'body contracts', one victim's full route, and how brokers lure workers to Russia who are then pushed into the army.

facts.statement: On the night of 13 November 2025 two boats heading for Europe sank off the Libyan coast; one carried 26 people from Bangladesh, of whom four died and the rest were rescued, according to Al Jazeera as reported by Prothom Alo on 17 November 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Al Jazeera via Prothom Alo, cited by columnist

facts.statement: Two of the dead, Enamul Sheikh (27) and Anis Sheikh (25) of Laokhanda village, Muksudpur, Gopalganj, left Bangladesh on 10 October 2025 and had paid a broker from Madaripur 21 lakh taka to go to Italy.

Munna Talukdar (19) of Madaripur made a 'body contract' of 22.5 lakh taka with a broker to reach Italy; his mother Rabeya Begum said the broker promised to get him to Italy by any means, took the 22.5 lakh taka and fled, and put him on a bad boat.

facts.statement: Route of Munna Talukdar's irregular journey to Italy: left home on 12 October 2025; taken first to Saudi Arabia where he performed Umrah; then to Kuwait for a few days; then Egypt; then by air to Benghazi, Libya; then to Misrata, Libya; on 1 November put on an engine boat from the Libyan coast towards Italy.

In December 2024 eight Bangladeshis died in a boat sinking.
facts.source_in_article: IOM via Business Standard (May 2024), cited by columnist

facts.statement: The columnist notes that detention and torture of migrants and refugees in Libya, ransom extraction and killings are regular occurrences, and that the Mediterranean crossing is one of the most dangerous routes.

Akram Hossain (25) of Sarail, Brahmanbaria, learned welding and went to Russia, but brokers enlisted him in the Russian army as a 'contract fighter'; after 15 days' training he was sent to Ukraine, where he was killed by a missile on 14 April 2025. His family had borrowed 7 lakh taka to send him to Russia.
Yasin Mia (22) of Gouripur, Mymensingh, went to Russia and was killed in a missile attack in April 2025 while fighting in Ukraine as a mercenary soldier.

According to a BRAC Migration Programme report cited in the column, brokers lure workers with false promises of high-paid jobs; many went to Russia hoping for work in oil, construction or logistics, and after arrival their passports are confiscated and they are forced to join the military. The columnist adds that some, finding the jobs they get do not pay off their debts, sign up as mercenaries for several times higher pay and are sent to the front after only 15 days' training.

After the deaths of Akram and Yasin, at least 10 families applied to the Bangladesh government to bring their relatives back from the Ukraine battlefield; the exact number of Bangladeshis fighting for Russia or killed and injured is not known.
The columnist warns that some Bangladeshis who chose to be mercenaries for Russia are promoting on social media the benefits of joining the Russian army.
The column says about 1 crore 10 lakh Bangladeshis, one seventeenth of the population, are abroad.

headline_en: Recruiting one lakh workers: Japanese delegation briefs Chief Adviser on progress
summary_en: A 23-member delegation of Japan's National Business Support Combined Cooperatives (NBCC) met Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus on 26 October 2025 to report progress on recruiting more than one lakh skilled Bangladeshi workers over five years. They gave year-by-year targets, the sectors in demand and said training is running at two centres in Khulna and Kapasia, Gazipur.

facts.statement: Japan's National Business Support Combined Cooperatives (NBCC), a Japanese business federation of more than 65 organisations, recently signed a memorandum with Bangladesh to set up a framework for training, certification and employment of Bangladeshis in Japan, aiming to recruit more than one lakh workers over the next five years under programmes such as the Technical Intern Training Program (TITP) and Specified Skilled Workers (SSW).
NBCC delegation members said that under the memorandum recruitment of 2,000 skilled workers in the first phase in 2026 is in process, followed by 6,000 in 2027 and 18,000 in 2028.

The Japanese delegates said workers are most needed in construction, services, aviation, garments and agriculture, and that demand for skilled drivers and for automobile and recycling workers will grow.
Prospective workers for Japan under the NBCC arrangement are being trained at two training centres, in Khulna and at Kapasia in Gazipur; NBCC delegates have visited both.

NBCC chairman Mikio Kesagayama said he visited the two training centres in March 2025 and found much progress seven months later, is very satisfied with the training and hopes to recruit 2,000 skilled workers in 2026, though the trainers' language skills could be improved.

Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus said language skill is the big challenge and suggested virtual classes by teachers from Japan and bringing Japanese trainers to Bangladesh; he said Bangladeshi women would excel in Japan's caregiving sector with language and other training.
NBCC representatives said Japan will need more than 4 lakh skilled nurses in the next few years and they will consider recruiting more nurses from Bangladesh.

Adviser Asif Nazrul said the government regularly reviews progress on recruitment to Japan, will prepare a specific roadmap, and the ministry has formed a dedicated cell to resolve problems in recruiting workers for Japan.

headline_en: Bangladesh has stepped up anti-trafficking measures: US TIP report
summary_en: The US State Department's 2025 Trafficking in Persons report keeps Bangladesh on Tier 2, saying it does not fully meet minimum standards but is making significant efforts. The article lists victim identification figures, the National Referral Mechanism, budget, BMET training centres including a 30-day course for women domestic workers, and labour agreements with Malaysia, South Korea and Brunei.

facts.statement: The US State Department's 2025 Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report places Bangladesh on Tier 2: the government does not fully meet the minimum standards for eliminating trafficking but is making significant efforts.

The government identified 1,462 trafficking victims: 144 trafficked for sex, 285 forced into labour and 1,033 victims of other forms of trafficking; the previous report recorded 1,210 identified victims.

Identified trafficking victims are given health care, legal aid and shelter through centres run by the ministries of women and children affairs, social welfare, and expatriates' welfare and overseas employment; the government formally adopted a National Referral Mechanism and trained police, immigration officers and labour inspectors on victim services.
The home ministry allocated 621.49 million taka in 2025 for trafficking prevention and awareness while continuing the National Plan of Action 2018-25, a significant increase on the previous year.
BMET continues to run 104 technical training centres and has introduced pre-departure training sessions for workers going abroad, including a specialised 30-day course for women domestic workers.

The report says Bangladesh strengthened bilateral labour agreements with Malaysia, South Korea and Brunei and established an employer-pays recruitment model to protect migrant workers from excessive fees.
A national policy for the social and economic reintegration of returnee migrant workers has been introduced; trafficking survivors are included so that they get livelihood opportunities after return.

The report notes Bangladesh's cooperation with Interpol, India, South Africa and others in investigating international trafficking networks, coordination among CID, PBI and CTTC, work with neighbours under a 2015 MoU with India on repatriating victims, and work with India, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand in the Bay of Bengal region.

headline_en: Two Rohingyas brought to Feni for trafficking; broker arrested with passports and NIDs
summary_en: A local broker in Feni was arrested on 3 August 2025 with two Rohingya refugees he and associates had brought from a Cox's Bazar camp on promises of Bangladeshi passports and passage abroad, after a failed attempt to traffic them to India via Parshuram. Police seized 3 Bangladeshi passports, 17 NIDs and birth certificates and filed a case.

facts.statement: At about 11pm on Sunday 3 August 2025 police, alerted by locals, detained broker Md Abdul Mannan (34) of Kalinagar, Parshuram upazila, Feni, and two Rohingyas from Balukhali camp, Ukhiya (Mohammad Arafat, 25, and Mosammat Ramida, 26) near the Mohipal passport office in Feni; 3 Bangladeshi passports, 17 NIDs and a number of birth registration certificates were seized from Mannan.

The two Rohingya refugees told police that broker Mannan and associates brought them from the camp to Feni by promising Bangladeshi passports and passage abroad; they were kept for a day in border-side Parshuram to be trafficked to India and, when that failed, brought back to Feni town.

Police filed a case naming three people including Abdul Mannan under the human trafficking prevention law and the passport and stamp forgery laws; Mannan was shown arrested and was to be sent to jail through court on Monday 4 August 2025, and the two Rohingyas were to be returned to the camp after legal process.

headline_en: An agreement will be signed with Saudi Arabia that even India and Pakistan do not have
summary_en: At a Remittance Fighters' Day event, adviser Asif Nazrul said a first-ever agreement on migrant workers with Saudi Arabia would be signed within two to three weeks. Returnees freed from Gulf jails after the July 2024 solidarity protests were honoured; 188 returnees from the UAE each got 50,000 taka, and 26 remain jailed in the UAE.

facts.statement: Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul said an agreement on migrant workers and employment is being signed with Saudi Arabia for the first time in history, to be known within two to three weeks; he said it will increase the safety and protection of workers there, the previous government failed to get it despite many attempts, and neither India nor Pakistan has such an agreement with Saudi Arabia.

Asif Nazrul urged people to go abroad only after informing themselves: people spend 8 to 10 lakh taka to go and many find no work on arrival; he said he saw migrant workers at one place in Saudi Arabia living in conditions worse than Bangladesh's worst slum.

Asif Nazrul said he was abused for arranging to send to Malaysia the workers who had earlier been unable to go; some migrants in Malaysia messaged that those who are undocumented there cannot regularise while more people are being brought from Bangladesh.

Senior secretary Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan said each of 188 workers who returned from the UAE after release from jail was given 50,000 taka, 94 lakh taka in total, and the ministry is working on their financial and social rehabilitation.

Three returnees from the UAE who spoke at the event said they want to go back to work and asked the government to free 26 people still imprisoned in the UAE (over solidarity protests with the July uprising).

The Chief Adviser's special envoy Lutfey Siddiqi said the UAE's pardon (of jailed Bangladeshi protesters) after one phone call from the Chief Adviser was a rare event; Asif Nazrul noted that under the strict laws of the UAE and Saudi Arabia migrants risked their livelihoods by showing solidarity with the movement.
Asif Nazrul said he strongly wishes to build a hospital for migrants.

headline_en: Migrant workers are dying at an average age of 37: RMMRU dialogue
summary_en: At a dialogue on 29 May 2025 held by the National Human Rights Commission and research body RMMRU, a paper analysing 554 dead migrants (2017 to October 2021) said their average age was 37 and 31 percent died unnatural deaths, and that 48 percent of families do not believe the cause on the death certificate. Speakers recommended post-mortems after bodies arrive, a mortuary at the airport and checks on pre-departure medical tests.

facts.statement: An RMMRU analysis of 554 dead Bangladeshi migrants from 2017 to October 2021 found their average age at death was 37; 31 percent died unnatural deaths (16 percent in accidents, 15 percent by suicide), 28 percent died natural deaths and the rest died of various diseases.
facts.source_in_article: RMMRU paper presented by Tasneem Siddiqui, 29 May 2025

facts.statement: The RMMRU paper says 40,713 workers died abroad in the past 12 years, and the bodies of 4,813 workers arrived in Bangladesh in 2024.

The Bangladesh government does no post-mortem to verify the death certificate sent with a migrant's body, although injury marks have been found on many bodies sent as natural deaths; 48 percent of dead migrants' families do not believe the cause on the death certificate, and the paper recommends post-mortem after the body arrives.

Senior secretary Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan of the expatriates' welfare ministry said post-mortem after arrival is possible, but the reaction of the country that sent the body if errors are found in the death certificate must be considered, as receiving countries, where lakhs of workers stay, may react adversely.

RMMRU acting executive director Tasneem Siddiqui said death certificates differ from country to country and often do not make the cause of death clear; families find wounds that the certificate does not mention, and a uniform certificate following WHO guidance could be arranged.

Recommendations in the RMMRU paper: a cold-storage mortuary at the airport to hold bodies for post-mortem, including dead workers' families in the returnee reintegration programme, and covering various diseases in pre-departure training.

Sajeda of Narsingdi worked for a year in a garment factory in Jordan and died in 2017; the family was told she suddenly fell from a building, and her brother Nur Mohammad wants to know the true cause.

Speakers said women migrants kill themselves after sexual abuse, and men kill themselves from despair at being unable to recover high migration costs despite extra work; many fall ill working 16 to 18 hours instead of 8.
Bodies are transported as cargo in coffins as in all countries; speakers said handover of bodies at Dhaka airport has been made easier and faster than before.

Former Human Rights Commission member Selim Reza said organ transplants are done in Middle Eastern countries and there are allegations of kidneys being taken from dying patients and sold; embassies must stay alert that no worker's organ is sold.

facts.statement: Forensic medicine specialist Kamrul Hasan said a post-mortem is essential to find the true cause of death and, given the ages at which workers die, every body should be examined; embassies should also investigate why workers die young.

summary_en: An editorial says worker departures to Saudi Arabia halved in February 2025 because a rule introduced on 22 December 2024 requires Bangladesh embassy attestation of every demand letter for more than one worker, where previously up to 24 needed none. It urges the ministry to act on BAIRA's demand to restore the old rule.

facts.statement: Under a rule the Bangladesh government introduced on 22 December 2024, a demand letter from Saudi Arabia for a single worker needs no attestation by the Bangladesh embassy there, but any demand letter for more than one worker must be attested; previously demand letters for up to 24 workers needed no embassy attestation.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial, citing BAIRA members

facts.statement: From October 2024 more than 80,000 workers a month on average went to Saudi Arabia, where demand rose after it was named host of the 2034 football World Cup; in February 2025 the number fell to half.

BAIRA members say 85 percent of workers going from Bangladesh to Saudi Arabia go on small demand letters of 1 to 24 workers, so visas cannot now be processed because of the embassy attestation delay; they demand a return to the old rule.

headline_en: Worker departures to Saudi Arabia falling because of attestation complication
summary_en: BAIRA members met adviser Asif Nazrul on 11 March 2025 over a 22 December 2024 rule requiring embassy attestation of all Saudi demand letters for more than one worker, which they say halved departures in February. They also asked that no syndicate be allowed again in the Malaysia market and demanded action against Amin Nur and Ruhul Amin alias Swapan.

facts.statement: The Bangladesh embassy in Saudi Arabia verifies and attests demand letters for workers; from 22 December 2024 a demand letter for one worker needs no embassy attestation but any for more than one does, whereas earlier up to 24 needed none. Former BAIRA joint secretary general Fakhrul Islam said that previously only BMET attestation was taken for up to 24 and the embassy lacks capacity to attest all.
facts.source_in_article: reporter; Fakhrul Islam, former joint secretary general, BAIRA

facts.statement: BMET sources: 44,229 workers went to Saudi Arabia in September 2024 and 83,582 in October 2024, staying at that level for three months; 76,618 went in January 2025 and 44,258 in February 2025.
BAIRA members say 85 percent of workers sent from Bangladesh to Saudi Arabia go on small demand letters of 1 to 24 workers, and visa processing is now stalled by the embassy attestation complication.

BAIRA members met expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul on Tuesday 11 March 2025 and said he would sit with all parties the next day to decide what to do; BAIRA leader Khandaker Abu Ashfaq said attesting every letter one by one takes much time and returning to the old rule would ease sending workers.

In a memorandum submitted to the ministry after a human chain on 5 February 2025, BAIRA members said the syndicate of Malaysian national Amin Nur and his Bangladeshi partner Ruhul Amin alias Swapan illegally extorted 1 lakh 7 thousand taka from every worker (going to Malaysia), and demanded strict legal action against them and steps so that no syndicate forms again.
BAIRA members said that under the previous government MPs and ministers formed a ring and plundered the Malaysia market, and asked that this not recur.
